organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: The hosts argue it has a dispersed but organized command structure with regional 'branches' or 'theaters'. Zawahiri is its emir.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula
organizations.notes: Wuhayshi led it and served as al-Qaeda general manager.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb
organizations.notes: Grew out of the GSPC. Said to have struck ceasefire-type deals with Mauritania and Burkina Faso.

organizations.name: Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin
aliases: Group for Support of Islam and Muslims
organizations.notes: Carried out suicide attacks in the 'Jerusalem will never be Judaized' campaign. Has current deals in central Mali.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: Carried out suicide attacks in the 'Jerusalem' campaign. A recent video on its Mogadishu assassination unit also praised lone-wolf attacks in the West.

organizations.name: Ansaru
organizations.notes: Active 2012 to about 2015, dormant, then re-emerged in 2019 in northwest Nigeria. Openly loyal to Zawahiri and AQIM.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent
organizations.notes: Hosts are unsure how Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind fits into its hierarchy.

organizations.name: Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind
organizations.notes: Founded in 2017 as a splinter of Hizbul Mujahideen by Zakir Musa. Named after the Ghazwat al-Hind hadith. It has had several leaders since Musa and has separate media from AQIS.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: An outgrowth of al-Qaeda in Iraq. Hosts call the split with al-Qaeda AQ's greatest defeat. It does not negotiate and has lost its physical caliphate.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Hosts say al-Qaeda and the Taliban are inextricably linked. Al-Qaeda supported the Taliban's negotiations with the US and its takeover.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Led by Sirajuddin Haqqani. Reported to be brokering Pakistan-Taliban talks in May 2022.

organizations.name: Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda supported its 2007 negotiations in Pakistan, which put it in control of significant portions of northern Pakistan (per the bin Laden files).

organizations.name: Hizbul Mujahideen
organizations.notes: Kashmir jihadist group. Its leader reportedly lives openly in Islamabad with the Pakistani establishment's support. Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind split from it.

organizations.name: Lashkar-e-Taiba
organizations.notes: Said to be the core of the 'Indian Mujahideen' branding. Fought alongside the Taliban in Afghanistan.

organizations.name: Harakat ul-Mujahideen
organizations.notes: Pakistani jihadist group focused on Kashmir that regrouped in Afghanistan to help the Taliban.

organizations.name: Indian Mujahideen
organizations.notes: Branding used in the 2000s and early 2010s for Pakistani groups' attacks in India, giving them plausible deniability.

organizations.name: Hamas
organizations.notes: Suppressed al-Qaeda-aligned groups in Gaza.

organizations.name: Palestinian Islamic Jihad
organizations.notes: One of the entrenched groups that blocked an al-Qaeda branch from forming in Palestine.

organizations.name: Palestinian Authority
organizations.notes: One of the entrenched groups that blocked an al-Qaeda branch from forming in Palestine.

organizations.name: Small Gaza AQ-affiliated group
organizations.notes: Shares AQ propaganda and sends condolences, but has not formally declared itself al-Qaeda. Name uncertain due to transcription.

organizations.name: Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Broke from the Taliban over the hiding of Mullah Omar's death, not over negotiations.

organizations.name: Salafist Group for Preaching and Combat
organizations.notes: Became AQIM. Abu Mohammed al-Yemini visited its training camps in Algeria and Mali.

organizations.name: Armed Islamic Group
organizations.notes: Cited as an example of division within the jihad. Also said to have been helped by al-Qaeda in the early 1990s.

organizations.name: Eritrean Islamic Jihad
organizations.notes: Helped by al-Qaeda in the early 1990s.

organizations.name: Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya
organizations.notes: Helped by al-Qaeda in the early 1990s.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in Iraq
organizations.notes: Historically the most problematic branch. It rebuffed the central leadership's request not to target Shia.

organizations.name: Free Syrian Army
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda's attempts at practical working relations with it, and with Turkey, in Syria backfired.

organizations.name: Islamic State Khorasan Province
organizations.notes: Claims rocket attacks on Uzbek and Tajik positions from Afghanistan. Seen as recruiting disaffected Central Asian and Uyghur fighters from AQ-aligned groups.

organizations.name: Turkistan Islamic Party
organizations.notes: Uyghur group that ultimately wants to wage jihad in China. Taliban closeness to China is a concern for its leadership. Some Uyghur members have reportedly left for ISK.

organizations.name: Pakistani military and intelligence establishment
organizations.notes: Supports Kashmir-focused groups and uses Kashmir as a relief valve for jihadists. Provided state aid to the Taliban. Dislikes al-Qaeda's independence.

organizations.name: Iran
organizations.notes: Provided state aid to the Taliban to wage jihad against the Americans.

organizations.name: Abu Sayyaf
organizations.notes: Mentioned as a group AQ-linked jihadism lost in the Philippines.

organizations.name: Jemaah Islamiyah
organizations.notes: Said to still exist to a degree in Southeast Asia.

events.description: Some analysts claimed Zawahiri was dead; the hosts say there was no evidence and he later reappeared in videos and audios.
Russia invaded Ukraine. Zawahiri's bin Laden commemoration speech refers to it, which establishes that he was alive as of that date.
Zawahiri speech commemorating Osama bin Laden, praising bin Laden's deeds and saying America is weak.
Al-Qaeda production on Kashmir and Palestine quoting Zawahiri, calling for jihad across the whole Indian subcontinent.
Al-Qaeda 'Jerusalem will never be Judaized' campaign (2020 or early 2021). al-Shabaab and JNIM carried out suicide attacks in its name.
Ansaru re-emerged in northwest Nigeria after a dormant period, openly loyal to Zawahiri and AQIM.
Zakir Musa founded Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind as an AQ-aligned splinter of Hizbul Mujahideen in Kashmir.
Zakir Musa was killed in an Indian military operation. Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind has had a series of less prominent leaders since.
Abu Mohammed al-Yemini was sent to Algeria and visited GSPC training camps in Algeria and Mali.
actors: Salafist Group for Preaching and Combat

events.description: In the early 1990s bin Laden sent people to East Africa, Sudan and Somalia to help train local insurgencies. Al-Qaeda helped the GIA, Eritrean Islamic Jihad and Al-Ihad.
Al-Qaeda supported the TTP's negotiations in Pakistan, which put the TTP in control of significant portions of northern Pakistan (per the bin Laden files).
Blaise Compaoré was ousted in Burkina Faso. He had reportedly had a deal with AQ.
AQ negotiated a ceasefire with Mauritania in the early 2000s, in return for Mauritania not attacking it.
Al-Qaeda negotiated with Iran to free an Iranian diplomat held in Pakistan, in exchange for greater freedom of movement for AQ leaders sheltering in Iran.

Reports that Sirajuddin Haqqani is brokering talks between Pakistan and the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) — the transcript says 'Afghan Taliban' but context is the Pakistan–TTP ceasefire talks hosted by the Afghan Taliban in Kabul.
Bin Laden was killed after about 10 years of searching, while sheltering in a Pakistani cantonment (year not stated in the transcript).
Zakir Musa founded Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind and led it from 2017 to 2019, openly aligning with al-Qaeda.
Zakir Musa was killed in an Indian military operation.
AQ and Zawahiri made statements urging Muslims in the Central African Republic to rise up and wage jihad; the effort failed (approximately 2014-2015).

key_claims: Zakir Musa founded AGH to align more closely with al-Qaeda; AGH has persisted through several leaders since his 2019 death despite lacking his prominence.
AGH's exact place in the AQIS hierarchy is unclear. It has separate media and may be a semi-autonomous sub-branch, like JNIM within AQIM.
The Pakistani state supports groups like LeT but is in conflict with AGH because AGH does not answer to it.
Pakistan uses Kashmir as a relief valve for jihadists, and after Afghanistan consolidates, Pakistani groups and AQ are expected to need new theaters such as Kashmir.
Central Asian jihadist groups in Afghanistan are largely under the al-Qaeda network. AQ must let them vent aggression without angering the Taliban or losing members to ISK.
The Turkistan Islamic Party faces the biggest rank-and-file pressure because the Taliban are cozying up to China, and some Uyghurs have reportedly defected to ISK.
Taking state aid from Pakistan and Iran gives the Taliban and AQ flexibility but lets IS portray them as tools of foreign states.

As of May 2022, AQ is in a stronger position than some analysts claim, though it failed in parts of Africa (Mozambique, DRC, Nigeria) and Southeast Asia, and its split with IS was its greatest defeat.
